passage:
The power went out at eleven, the night before the accounts exam, and the hostel generator coughed and died. Ankita and Jyoti gave up revising by phone torch and lay on their beds in the dark.
"Can I tell you something?" Ankita said. "My parents barely speak now. Papa sleeps at the shop some nights." She waited, heart loud, for Jyoti to change the subject.
Jyoti didn't. "That sounds so lonely for you," she said. After a pause: "I'm scared I'll fail this course and my mother will say she knew it." Then, quieter: "And I still check my ex's profile. Two years later. Pathetic."
"Not pathetic," Ankita said. "I did the same with mine for a whole summer."
When the lights came back at one, neither of them reached for their notes straight away. They'd have to cram at dawn, but it felt as if they'd both passed a test they hadn't studied for.

qa.q: When did the lights come back?
qa.a: The lights came back at one.

qa.q: Why did Ankita wait with her heart loud after speaking?
qa.a: Ankita was afraid Jyoti might change the subject; she was checking whether Jyoti would respond with care.

qa.q: What made this conversation deepen the friendship?
qa.a: Each disclosure was met with care and matched: Jyoti named Ankita's loneliness and shared her own fears, and Ankita answered 'Not pathetic' with a story of her own. 🤍

qa.q: What would change if Jyoti had changed the subject?
qa.a: Ankita would likely feel exposed and pull back, and the friendship might have stayed on the surface instead of becoming real.

grounding: Shows two hostel friends trading family troubles, career fears and old heartbreak, each watching whether the other responds with care.

passage:
The bakery near the college gate in Hyderabad was nearly empty at four. Rehana stirred her tea for too long before she said it: her engagement had been called off in the summer, and her khala still brought it up at every family dinner.
Jyoti put down her puff. She'd known Rehana for five months, mostly as a lab partner. For a second she didn't know what to say, then chose honesty. "I didn't know. I'm sorry. That must feel like it's on display all the time."
Rehana nodded, eyes on the cup.
Jyoti took a breath. "Can I tell you mine? I'm terrified I won't get placed. Papa's shop closed in March and everyone's counting on me."
Rehana looked up properly then. "You carry that into lab every day, alone?"
They stayed till the owner started stacking chairs. On the walk to the bus stop, Jyoti kept thinking: she told me first, and she didn't flinch at mine.

qa.q: What did Rehana share about the summer?
qa.a: Rehana said her engagement had been called off in the summer.

qa.q: What was Jyoti thinking on the walk to the bus stop?
qa.a: Jyoti felt trusted and safe: Rehana had told her first and didn't flinch at her fears, so the friendship now felt real.

qa.q: How did Jyoti respond in a way that helped Rehana trust her?
qa.a: Jyoti named how exposed Rehana must feel instead of giving advice, then shared a fear of her own, so the openness went both ways.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt when Jyoti shared her placement fear?
qa.a: Rehana probably felt less alone and more trusted, and saw that Jyoti thought of her as a real friend, not just a lab partner.

grounding: Illustrates two young women deepening a friendship through matched disclosures about heartbreak, family pressure and career fear, each checking for care.
